source.title: Neuron Populations Exhibit Divergent Selectivity with Scale
source.authors: Amil Dravid; Yasaman Bahri; Alexei A. Efros; Yossi Gandelsman

page_placements.theme: Scale and fine-tuning trends in neuron monosemanticity proxies

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether explanations inferred from activating examples predict held-out neuron activations, using a different measure and setting from the claim’s proposed audit.
record.gate_note: The paper measures Rosetta-neuron counts and selectivity across model scales, but these are not the claim’s stated fractions of neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or unknown jobs. Its held-out prediction validation is the result that directly bears on V6. Matching-rule choices and results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Section H.3 asks whether a description inferred from a neuron's top-20 activating images predicts which unseen images activate it. This bears directly, though weakly, on V6, using vision neurons and a different method from the original. It is framed as validation of the authors' VLM judge. The Rosetta scaling, kurtosis and monosemanticity-rate results do not measure any version's stated shares.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that Rosetta neurons follow a sublinear power law and become more selective and domain-specialized with scale, while non-Rosetta neurons stay polysemantic. They validate the VLM judge as above chance and caution that the selectivity measures are proxies showing relative trends.
record.recipe_differences: The held-out validation uses a VLM to infer a feature from top-activating vision examples and predict activation on unseen images; it is not the original Qwen3 neuron-pole audit or a text-neuron explanation-score simulation.
record.method_sensitivity: The vision monosemanticity judgment rate decreases as the number of top-activating images shown increases; the gap between Rosetta and non-Rosetta neurons remains stable, and estimates begin to stabilize around k=20 (Section H.2, Figure 36).

fits_no_version.finding: Rosetta Neuron counts grow sublinearly with model size (exponents about 0.5–0.7) in language and vision families.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model-matched neuron counts scale sublinearly with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Rosetta neurons become more selective with scale while non-Rosetta neurons stay or become less selective. Measured by kurtosis in language models and VLM-judged monosemanticity in vision models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling polarizes neurons into a growing selective shared population and a polysemantic background.

record.problems: Selectivity is operationalized using modality-specific proxies; the vision metric relies on GPT-5.4 judgments. The held-out predictive validation is for vision neurons from OpenCLIP ViT-B/16 and does not establish how well text-neuron explanations predict text activations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out. Other reported results, such as document-type firing and data filtering, do not measure the claim versions’ stated neuron-pole shares or held-out explanation prediction.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or one-job, two-job and unknown shares.
No one-job shares for language models. Kurtosis is not a share. Models go only up to about 32B, and none are mixture-of-experts.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic-neuron reanalysis.
No comparison of interpretable share across tools or architectures. The DINOv3 exception concerns Rosetta counts, not interpretability share.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
No text neurons. There is no test beyond a top-versus-bottom-half contrast, and no comparison of judged 'one job' with prediction quality per neuron.
No simulation-based scoring of explanations on new text.

missing.what: Monosemanticity rates judged by the VLM fall as more top-activating images are shown (k from 2 to 50). Judgments from few examples therefore rate more neurons monosemantic than judgments from more examples, which bears on V6's inspection-overstatement point. Values are figure-only.

record.verdict_notes: The V6 evidence comes from a metric-validation experiment on vision neurons with an easy held-out contrast. It shows that explanations from top examples mostly but imperfectly predict firing, so the support is weak. The paper never claims or tests a share of neurons with one main job in language models.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or estimates of the one-job, two-job, and not-understood fractions.
Does not measure the stated shares of neuron poles; models reach about 30B parameters, not trillions, and the text does not identify mixture-of-experts models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.

Does not compare interpretability shares under different tools or test the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates. It discusses a DINOv3 scaling exception, but does not test the version’s stated share estimates.
No attribution-graph reconstruction or comparison with a trained replacement model.
Tests held-out prediction from top-activating examples for vision-model neurons, not text neurons or whether the specific one-job pole audit overstates its coverage.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating their activations on new text or report the share of neurons receiving good scores.

rows.subject: GPT-5.4
rows.operation_detail: Predicts which held-out images activate a neuron from its top-activating images and activation maps.

conditions.value: 100 random neurons from OpenCLIP ViT-B/16 per trial
5 independent trials, each with a disjoint subset of 100 neurons
top 20 activating images with activation maps
10 shuffled raw images: 5 next-highest-activating and 5 random images from the bottom 50% of activations

rows.measure: Accuracy on held-out image activation prediction
rows.note: The score is above chance but below perfect prediction; the study presents this as evidence that the VLM judge is predictive.
rows.check: Row is correct. The held-out set is easy: 5 next-highest activators versus 5 from the bottom 50%. It cannot show failures on mid-range or out-of-distribution inputs. Neurons are random OpenCLIP ViT-B/16 neurons, a vision model.
